proposals.name: Fisherwitches
proposals.entry:
Common Names: Fisherwitches, Dock Wives, Net Mothers
Found In: The Shambles docks, particularly the Iron Docks
Occupation: Fishmongers, net-menders, salvagers, midwives, fish-dressers, dock laborers
Reputation: Unpleasant, indispensable, probably witches

“Never insult a Fisherwitch while your boat is still in the water.”

The Fisherwitches are the hard-faced women of the Shambles docks who gut Fogport's fish, mend its nets, haul its stranger catches ashore, and know considerably more about the harbor than respectable people would prefer.

Nobody knows precisely when people began calling them witches.

The Fisherwitches certainly don't object.

They work in small crews of sisters, cousins, daughters, widows, adopted strays, and women whose exact relationship to one another becomes increasingly difficult to determine after three generations.

They are recognizable by their dark work dresses, heavy boots, and peculiar high-pointed oilskin shawls, folded and waxed against the rain until their silhouettes resemble crooked black steeples.

They are loud, rude, superstitious, extremely difficult to embarrass, and notorious for laughing at inappropriate moments.

The Iron Docks

Fisherwitches can be found anywhere fish are landed in the Shambles, but the Iron Docks are theirs.

Before dawn they arrive with hooks, buckets, knives, nets, lanterns, and pots of terrible tea.

They clean ordinary catches.

They butcher enormous catches.

And when Fogport fishermen drag something onto the dock that nobody can identify, somebody invariably says:

“Fetch the witches.”

This is where their reputation becomes deserved.

A Fisherwitch may examine an unknown creature's eyes, smell its gills, stick a finger into its mouth, ask where it was caught, and pronounce:

“Don't eat the yellow bits.”

Usually this is excellent advice.

What They Know

The Fisherwitches possess generations of accumulated practical knowledge about the waters around Fogport.

They know which fish arrive before storms.

They recognize diseases by the smell of a gill.

They know which things are poisonous, which merely look poisonous, and which remain dangerous several hours after being chopped apart.

They know currents that do not appear on charts.

They know where wreckage washes ashore.

They know which boats came home lighter than they departed.

Most importantly, they notice changes.

If something new has begun swimming beneath Fogport, the Fisherwitches will probably know before the Civic Order does.

Getting them to explain what they know is another matter.

Are They Actually Witches?

Probably.

But not in the manner respectable Fogporters imagine.

Their practices consist mostly of folk medicine, weather lore, sailor superstition, inherited recipes, obscure anatomy, and an alarming willingness to touch things everyone else has sensibly backed away from.

They tie knots over sickbeds.

They hang fish jaws above doors.

They spit into the harbor before launching a boat.

They sometimes whisper into the mouths of dead fish.

A Fisherwitch might prescribe eel fat for a rash and then tell you never to pronounce your mother's name while standing in seawater.

The eel fat works.

Nobody particularly wants to test the other part.

Licensed Luminati generally dismiss Fisherwitch practices as superstition.

Fisherwitches generally dismiss licensed Luminati as “lamp-backed university bastards.”

The Pointed Shawls

The shawls are practical garments made from layers of waxed cloth, sail scraps, fish leather, and whatever else keeps the rain out.

The exaggerated point is traditional.

Different folds once indicated families, docks, marital status, or occupation, although almost nobody outside the Fisherwitches can still read them correctly.

A Fisherwitch without her shawl is simply working.

A Fisherwitch who deliberately removes her shawl before speaking to you is another matter.

Among dockworkers, this is taken as a sign that the conversation has become serious.

Children of the Docks

Children are frequently present among Fisherwitch crews.

They learn young.

A six-year-old may sort shellfish. An eight-year-old can mend a net. By twelve, many can identify dangerous harbor creatures more reliably than a Collegium naturalist.

The Fisherwitches are fiercely protective of these children.

Nobody on the Iron Docks interferes with one lightly.

There is an old Shambles story about a dock foreman who struck a Fisherwitch girl.

According to the story, he drowned three days later in a puddle.

The Fisherwitches insist this is ridiculous.

There wasn't nearly enough water in the puddle.

Reputation

The Shambles treats the Fisherwitches with an unusual combination of mockery, affection, and caution.

Fishermen bring them strange catches.

Pregnant women sometimes seek their advice.

Smugglers ask about tides.

Murderers occasionally ask what sinks.

The Civic Order mostly ignores them.

This arrangement suits the Fisherwitches perfectly.

posts.name: Gamemaster Only
posts.entry:
The Fisherwitches Are an Information Network

The Fisherwitches should be useful recurring contacts rather than simply spooky background characters.

Their great advantage is observation.

Hundreds of eyes pass through the docks every day: wives waiting for boats, children sorting catches, old women repairing nets, fishmongers purchasing stock.

They don't spy.

They work.

Consequently they see almost everything entering Fogport from the water.

Byl and Lott can learn a great deal from them, provided they are willing to tolerate insults, perform favors, or help drag something disgusting across a dock.

The Thing in the Net

One morning the Fisherwitches quietly close part of the Iron Docks.

No Civic Order officers are summoned.

They have caught something.

It looks like an enormous malformed fish.

Then someone discovers clothing inside its stomach.

Not scraps.

An intact coat.

Inside the coat is an object belonging to someone Byl and Lott know.

The Fisherwitches insist the creature could not possibly have swallowed its victim at sea.

The fish has never been in salt water.

So where did it come from?

The Empty Boats

The Fisherwitches notice that boats from one particular stretch of coastline are returning strangely clean.

No barnacles.

No weeds.

No small fish in their nets.

Nothing.

The fishermen themselves insist everything is normal.

Then one boat returns without its crew.

Its deck is wet.

Its nets are neatly folded.

Dinner is still warm below deck.

One Fisherwitch refuses to step aboard.

She recognizes the smell.

A Favor for Byl

One of the older Fisherwitches knows exactly what Byl is.

Not his history.

Not necessarily his true name.

She recognizes a wild magician.

She doesn't report him.

Instead she asks for a favor.

Something has been happening to one of the Fisherwitch children: small objects move while she sleeps, fish die when she becomes frightened, and once every lamp on a dock went dark when she screamed.

The Fisherwitches will not surrender the girl to the Collegium.

They want Byl to tell them whether she is dangerous.

This puts Byl in the uncomfortable position of being treated as the nearest available expert on illegal magic.

Lott Is Popular

The Fisherwitches like Lott.

They feed him.

Nobody remembers how this began.

One of them discovers that Lott will happily carry enormous baskets of fish, and from that moment onward the relationship is settled.

They shout greetings at him across the docks.

They occasionally give him smoked fish wrapped in newspaper.

One ancient Fisherwitch insists he is too thin.

This is obviously absurd.

She continues feeding him.

Their affection becomes useful when Byl and Lott need somewhere on the docks where Civic Vigilance officers are unlikely to receive cooperative answers.

Something Has Been Eating the Rats

The Fisherwitches are the first to notice.

There are fewer rats along one stretch of the Iron Docks.

Then there are none.

The Rat Catchers congratulate themselves.

The Fisherwitches do not.

Whatever is eating the rats has begun taking cats.

One Fisherwitch has seen its tracks.

They begin at the water.

They do not return to it.

The Drowned Witch

A Fisherwitch is found dead beneath the Iron Docks.

Everyone assumes she fell.

Her sisters know better.

Before burial, they discover something sewn into the pointed tip of her shawl: a tiny waterproof packet containing three names and a rough map.

One name belongs to a smuggler.

One belongs to a Civic Order official.

The third is Lott.

Nobody knows why.

The dead woman had never apparently met him.

The Old Rule

There is one piece of Fisherwitch superstition that should eventually prove completely correct:

Never bring ashore a fish that calls you by name.

The Fisherwitches do not know why.

They only know that their grandmothers taught them this, and their grandmothers learned it from theirs.

Eventually, somewhere in the Sayir Sea, a fisherman hears his name spoken softly from inside his net.

And makes the mistake of answering.
